country_team.q27.value: Hands-on guidance and local experience are particularly important during the proposal development, project implementation, monitoring, and sustainability phases of the project cycle. During proposal development, local guidance helps applicants better understand donor requirements, align project ideas with national priorities, and develop realistic approaches based on local conditions. During implementation, continuous technical support and sharing of local experiences are important to address practical challenges, adapt activities when needed, and ensure effective stakeholder engagement. Local experience is also critical during monitoring, evaluation, and post-project sustainability planning, as it helps assess the long-term effectiveness of interventions and identify mechanisms to maintain project outcomes beyond the funding period. While global guidelines provide important overall direction, their successful application often requires adaptation to the national context.

country_team.q28.value: Financial constraints are a key barrier to effective learning from other country teams, particularly for facilitating direct interactions, experience-sharing events, and peer-learning activities. While online platforms and data-sharing mechanisms provide useful information, they often provide limited insights into practical experiences, challenges, and context-specific solutions. Direct engagement and exchange among country teams are more valuable for understanding real-world implementation experiences.

country_team.q29.value: The most useful support would have been timely, practical guidance on adapting global programme requirements and procedures to the national context, particularly during the initial stages of implementation. While operational manuals, the Country Programme Strategy (CPS), and reference documents provide important information, practical examples, templates, and experiences from other country teams would have been valuable in understanding how similar challenges were addressed in real implementation contexts. Such support would help ensure more effective application of requirements, improve consistency in proposal review and project management, and reduce the time required to interpret and adapt global guidance to country-level needs.

country_team.q27.value: As the SGP Cambodia team, we have found that hands-on guidance and local experience are most critical during project design, implementation, and monitoring stages, although they add value throughout the entire project cycle. Project Design and Development: Local experience is essential in ensuring that project ideas are aligned with community needs, local priorities, environmental realities, and cultural practices. Many community-based organizations have strong technical knowledge of local issues but may need practical guidance to translate their ideas into clear project objectives, realistic workplans, budgets, and measurable indicators. Early hands-on support helps improve project quality and increases the likelihood of successful implementation. Project Implementation: This is the stage where hands-on guidance is often most important. Communities frequently face operational challenges, such as technical issues, stakeholder coordination, procurement, financial management, and adapting activities to changing local conditions. Regular field engagement and mentoring help project teams troubleshoot problems, make informed decisions, and maintain momentum while ensuring compliance with SGP requirements. Monitoring, Learning, and Adaptive Management: Local experience plays a key role in understanding whether project activities are producing meaningful results on the ground. Direct engagement with communities allows for timely identification of challenges, lessons learned, and opportunities for adaptive management. Hands-on support also strengthens community capacity in data collection, reporting, and documenting impacts, ensuring that project achievements and lessons are accurately captured. Why it matters: SGP projects are community-driven and often implemented in diverse socio-economic and ecological contexts. Local knowledge helps bridge the gap between project design and ground realities, while hands-on guidance builds the capacity and confidence of community organizations. Together, they improve project effectiveness, sustainability, ownership, and long-term impact beyond the project period. In our experience, while all stages benefit from local expertise, the implementation phase requires the greatest level of hands-on guidance because this is where project plans are translated into tangible actions and where most practical challenges emerge.

country_team.q28.value: The main barriers to learning from other country teams are often differences in local contexts, limited time and resources, language barriers, and the lack of structured opportunities for regular knowledge exchange. While many lessons and good practices are shared across countries, it can be difficult to determine how applicable they are to Cambodia's specific environmental, socio-economic, policy, and community conditions. In addition, country teams are often managing multiple priorities, leaving limited time to review lengthy reports or participate in frequent knowledge-sharing activities. A peer network would be worth using if it provides practical, timely, and easily accessible solutions to common challenges faced by SGP country teams. The most valuable features would include: Real-life case studies and lessons learned from similar projects and contexts. Direct peer-to-peer exchange, allowing country teams to ask questions and receive practical advice from colleagues with relevant experience. Simple and searchable knowledge resources, such as templates, tools, methodologies, and success stories. Thematic communities of practice where teams working on similar issues (biodiversity, climate change, sustainable livelihoods, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, etc.) can regularly interact. Opportunities for learning visits, webinars, and mentoring that focus on practical implementation challenges rather than only reporting outcomes. In our view, a successful peer network should prioritize actionable knowledge and direct engagement among practitioners, helping country teams quickly adapt proven approaches while acknowledging differences in local contexts. This would strengthen learning, improve project delivery, and avoid duplication of effort across the SGP network.

country_team.q29.value: If there were one type of information or support that would have been most useful at the right time, it would be practical, on-demand technical and implementation guidance from peers who have faced similar challenges. While guidance documents and templates are helpful, country teams and grantees often encounter specific issues during project implementation that require context-based solutions. Having quick access to peer experiences, practical examples, and expert advice on topics such as community engagement, project adaptation, innovative livelihood models, biodiversity conservation approaches, and results measurement would help teams address challenges more efficiently and avoid repeating mistakes. This type of support is particularly valuable because SGP projects operate in dynamic and diverse local contexts where unforeseen issues frequently arise. Timely access to proven approaches and lessons learned from other country teams can improve decision-making, strengthen project implementation, save time and resources, and enhance overall project outcomes. In the Cambodia context, learning from peers who have successfully implemented similar interventions in community-based conservation, Indigenous Peoples and local community engagement, and sustainable livelihood initiatives would have been especially beneficial for strengthening project effectiveness and scaling successful practices.

country_team.q27.value: During procurement and implementation, close guidance is often essential, particularly for smaller civil society organisations that may have limited experience with formal procedures. The National Coordinator helps grantees understand requirements, avoid delays, identify practical solutions and adjust activities when difficulties arise. The National Coordinator also brings knowledge from other projects and from many years of programme experience. This makes it possible to share proven approaches, connect organisations facing similar challenges, introduce new ideas and encourage innovation. In many cases, the strongest ideas do not emerge from a single project alone, but from combining the grantee's local knowledge with lessons learned across the wider SGP portfolio. This hands-on support is therefore important throughout the entire project cycle, as it helps ensure that projects remain realistic, compliant, innovative and capable of delivering meaningful results.

country_team.q28.value: The main barrier is the lack of time and human resources. The country programme is managed by a single National Coordinator on a continuous, rolling basis. While one group of projects is being implemented, monitored and supported, financial reports must also be reviewed in detail, including the verification of hundreds of small invoices and receipts. At the same time, a new call for proposals must be launched, applicants guided in developing new projects, proposals reviewed, and projects prepared for approval and contracting. Typically, around 10 projects may be under implementation in any given year within a four-year operational cycle, while a new generation of projects is simultaneously being developed. In parallel, the National Coordinator must remain closely connected to developments on the ground, participate in networking events and strategic meetings, maintain relationships with key stakeholders, and continuously deepen their understanding of the country's evolving sustainable development and environmental challenges. This engagement is essential for identifying emerging needs, developing relevant initiatives and positioning the Programme strategically. It is extremely difficult for one person to provide adequate oversight and hands-on support across such a large and constantly evolving portfolio while also fulfilling the Programme's administrative, financial, reporting, networking and strategic responsibilities. This leaves very limited time for structured learning and exchange with other countries. A peer network would be worth using if it provided quick, practical and easily searchable support. It should enable National Coordinators to identify colleagues with relevant experience, access tested tools and examples, and obtain concise advice on specific challenges without adding further meetings, reporting obligations or administrative workload.

country_team.q29.value: The most useful support would have been dedicated administrative and financial capacity to remove the administrative burden from the National Coordinator. A significant amount of time is currently spent reviewing financial reports, checking hundreds of invoices and receipts, following procurement and contracting procedures, processing documentation, and meeting multiple administrative and reporting requirements. These functions are necessary, but they considerably reduce the time available for the National Coordinator's core responsibilities: providing hands-on support to grantees, monitoring projects in the field, developing new initiatives, maintaining strategic partnerships, participating in relevant networks and building a deep understanding of the country's evolving sustainable development challenges. The timely provision of programme, administrative and financial support, or the centralisation and simplification of these functions, would therefore have had the greatest impact. It would allow the National Coordinator to concentrate on the strategic, technical and relationship-building role that adds the most value to the Programme and its grantees.

country_team.q28.value: To enhance the effectiveness of projects and to foster a culture of continuous learning, I recommend the establishment of a share communication group via Microsoft Team. This platform would serve as a centralized hub for project teams across the country to share information, exchange experiences, and collaboratively solve common challenges. The key benefits of such a platform would be: • New project teams can learn from the successes and failures of their peers, avoiding common pitfalls and adopting best practices from the outset. • A collective forum for questions and answers would enable teams to tap into a wider pool of expertise to solve pressing issues in a timely manner. • The platform would foster a sense of community and encourage collaboration between teams, potentially leading to joint initiatives and greater collective impact.

country_team.q27.value: In my experience, hands-on guidance and local experience are particularly important during proposal development, project review, implementation planning, and monitoring. At the proposal stage, local knowledge helps ensure that projects are well aligned with the GEF focal areas and national priorities, while also reflecting the actual needs and context of local communities. It is also important to ensure strong ownership and participation of CBOs/CSOs throughout the project cycle. Hands-on guidance can help them develop realistic approaches for employment generation, sustainable livelihoods, community ownership, and long-term sustainability beyond the project period. During implementation and monitoring, local experience is critical for identifying challenges early, adapting activities to the local context, and ensuring that project interventions remain practical, relevant, and sustainable.

country_team.q28.value: The main barriers are limited time, differences in country contexts, competing priorities, and limited opportunities for structured exchange. Although country teams may face similar challenges, approaches and solutions are not always directly transferable because of differences in institutional arrangements, policies, resources, and local circumstances. A peer network would be most valuable if it provides practical, experience-based learning rather than only sharing information. Regular opportunities to exchange lessons learned, tools, templates, good practices, and challenges; access to peers who have addressed similar issues; and focused discussions around specific project-cycle challenges would make the network useful. A simple and well-maintained platform, supported by regular engagement and clear follow-up, would also encourage continued participation and help translate peer learning into practical action.

country_team.q29.value: The most useful support would have been timely, practical guidance and lessons learned from similar projects or country teams, particularly when making key implementation decisions.
